title: Highest-Protein Fish: A Clear Ranking per 100 Grams

seo.title: Highest-Protein Fish per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: Compare cooked tuna, mackerel, trout, swordfish, cod and salmon by protein, calories and serving, with clear mercury context.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked fish by protein without mixing canned and fresh products.

excerpt: Cooked yellowfin tuna leads clearly at about 29 g of protein per 100 g. Most of the other fish here fall between roughly 20 and 24 g, so calories, omega-3 fat and, for certain species and groups, mercury often matter more than a one-gram protein difference.
content_html:
If you are looking for the fish with the most protein, yellowfin tuna stands out clearly. After that, the gaps become much smaller: mackerel, trout, swordfish, cod and salmon are separated by only a few grams of protein.

The next table keeps the comparison consistent by using cooked fish per 100 grams. Canned and salted products come later because draining, oil, water loss and salt can substantially change both concentration and calories.

Protein and calories per 100 g cooked

FishProteinCalories
Yellowfin tuna29.2 g130
Atlantic mackerel23.9 g262
Farmed rainbow trout23.8 g168
Swordfish23.5 g172
Wild rainbow trout22.9 g150
Atlantic cod22.8 g105
Farmed Atlantic salmon22.1 g206
Haddock20.0 g90

Two things matter more than the exact order of every row. First, tuna is genuinely higher: it provides about 5–9 g more protein per 100 g than the other fish listed. Second, among fish clustered around 22–24 g, ranking by tenths of a gram creates a precision that usually does not matter at the table.

Mackerel and cod are a good example. They provide 23.9 and 22.8 g protein — only 1.1 g apart — but 262 versus 105 calories per 100 g. That much larger difference is mostly about fat.

Tuna: high protein with relatively few calories

Cooked yellowfin tuna provides about 29.2 g protein and 130 calories per 100 g. A 5-ounce / 142 g serving supplies roughly 41 g protein, so it is a very concentrated protein food without much fat.

That does not mean every product called “tuna” has the same nutrient profile or the same mercury guidance. Species and product type matter, especially for pregnant or breastfeeding people and children.

Mackerel, salmon and cod: similar protein, very different fat

Atlantic mackerel provides about 23.9 g protein and 262 calories per 100 g; farmed Atlantic salmon about 22.1 g and 206 calories; cod about 22.8 g and 105 calories. Salmon and cod differ by only 0.7 g protein, but salmon is about 100 calories higher per 100 g.

The main reason is fat. Salmon commonly contains more than 10–12 g fat per 100 g, while cod is close to 1 g. Mackerel and salmon also provide EPA and DHA long-chain omega-3 fats. A higher calorie number is therefore not automatically a disadvantage; it reflects a different nutritional package.

Trout sits in the middle

Farmed rainbow trout is around 23.8 g protein per 100 g and wild rainbow trout about 22.9 g. In a 5-ounce / 142 g serving, that is roughly 34 versus 33 g protein — a difference of about one gram.

For a real meal, taste, price, availability and fat content are likely to matter more than that small protein gap.

Mercury can matter more than the protein ranking

Mercury does not track protein. A fish can provide about 23 g protein and still come with different consumption advice because of the species. Swordfish is the clearest example here: it provides about 23.5 g protein per 100 g, almost the same as trout and mackerel, but FDA/EPA places swordfish in its “Choices to Avoid” category for people who are pregnant or breastfeeding and for children.

Tuna also needs species-level context. FDA/EPA lists canned light tuna among “Best Choices,” albacore/white tuna among “Good Choices,” and bigeye tuna among “Choices to Avoid” for those groups. The word “tuna” by itself is not enough to describe mercury exposure.

For most adults, protein can be one useful comparison. For groups who need to pay closer attention to mercury, the exact species can be more important than gaining one or two extra grams of protein.

Fresh cod, salted cod and canned fish are different products

The cooked fresh cod in the table provides about 22.8 g protein and 105 calories per 100 g. Salted cod loses water during curing and becomes much higher in sodium; desalting changes it again. It should not be treated as nutritionally identical to simply cooked fresh cod.

Canned fish changes for similarly concrete reasons. Drained sardines in oil provide about 24.6 g protein per 100 g, and drained anchovies can approach 28.9 g. Less water makes the protein more concentrated, while added oil can raise calories and salt can raise sodium substantially.

Serving size changes the picture too. Twenty grams of anchovies provides about 5.8 g protein. A high per-100-g number does not mean anchovies are usually eaten in the same quantity as a fish fillet.

Protein in a normal serving

FishServingProtein
Cooked tuna5 oz / 142 g41 g
Mackerel5 oz / 142 g34 g
Trout5 oz / 142 g34 g
Cod5 oz / 142 g32 g
Salmon5 oz / 142 g31 g
Canned sardines3.75 oz can / ~106 g~26 g

At a normal serving size, mackerel, trout, cod and salmon still cluster closely at about 31–34 g protein. Tuna remains the one that clearly separates itself, at roughly 41 g in a 5-ounce serving.

So which fish is best if protein is the goal?

For a lot of protein with relatively few calories, tuna, cod and haddock perform especially well. If you also want more long-chain omega-3 fat, salmon and mackerel provide similar protein to cod but come with more fat and energy.

If mercury guidance applies to you or your child, the exact species matters more than a small difference in the ranking. The useful takeaway is not that one fish wins every category, but that some protein differences are meaningful while many others are too small to outweigh fat, omega-3s, mercury, sodium in processed products, price or preference.

faq.question: Which fish has the most protein?
faq.answer: Among the cooked fish compared here, yellowfin tuna is about 29.2 g/100 g. Mackerel, trout, swordfish and cod cluster around 22.8–23.9 g.

faq.question: Does salmon have less protein than tuna?
faq.answer: Yes in these examples: about 22.1 g/100 g versus 29.2 g for yellowfin tuna. Salmon contains much more fat, including omega-3s.

faq.question: Which fish are highest in mercury?
faq.answer: FDA/EPA places swordfish and bigeye tuna among the choices to avoid for pregnant or breastfeeding people and children.
